::: {.fs-80}
The first cell lists the columns of `europeanisation`, with the type and the first values of each; the second counts countries, years and rows.\
**In the IDE workspace:** the chunk `count-data` of `index.qmd`.

```

c(countries = insight::n_unique(europeanisation$cntry), years = insight::n_unique(europeanisation$year),
  rows = nrow(europeanisation))
```
:::

::: notes
The panel is already loaded in the slides as `europeanisation`, as it is in your report. The first cell lists its thirteen columns with their types and first values: the country by name and by code, the year, the six framing scales as means of each country-year, the respondent count behind each mean, GDP growth, the unemployment rate and the bailout marker. The outcome that we take first is `mcosmo`, the mean cosmopolitan framing on a scale from nought to one, and the predictor is `unemp`, the annual unemployment rate. [run both] The second cell counts twenty-seven countries, ten years and two hundred and seventy rows, as the chunk `count-data` does in your report, and the codebook beside the data file describes every column.

## Hands-on 2 – Framing by country {#hands-on-2-framing-by-country .smaller .output-figure}

::: {.fs-80}
**In the IDE workspace:** the chunk `fig-cosmo-trend` of `index.qmd`, which draws the same figure.
:::

::: {.fs-80}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| max-lines: 3
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4
# the lines first, one panel per country, then the points added on top
tinyplot::tinyplot(
  mcosmo ~ year, facet = ~cntry, data = europeanisation, type = "l", col = "grey55",
  facet.args = list(ncol = 6), xaxb = c(2004, 2008, 2013), theme = "minimal",
  main = "Cosmopolitan EU framing by country, 2004–2013",
  xlab = "", ylab = "Mean cosmopolitan framing"
)
tinyplot::tinyplot_add(type = "p", col = "black", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
```
:::

::: notes
This is the outcome over time, one small panel per country, drawn by tinyplot with the graphics of base R, the lines first and the points on top, as the chunk `fig-cosmo-trend` of your report draws it. [run it] In most countries the framing changes little over the decade, while in a few it moves sharply around the crisis of 2009. The fixed-effects models of Task 3 use that variation within a country over time, so find two or three countries that move and note them in a comment in your report, since they carry the estimate.
:::

## Hands-on 2 – The estimand {#hands-on-2-the-estimand .smaller}

::: {.small}
Before fitting anything, say what you are trying to estimate, in words. A template that you can adapt:
:::

::: {.fs-85}
> The **unit-specific quantity** is the change in mean cosmopolitan EU framing within a country from one year to another associated with a one-point change in that country's unemployment rate. The **target population** is EU member states over 2004–2013. The **aggregation** is a weighted average of those unit-specific effects, in which the country-years whose unemployment departs most from their country and year means count most, holding fixed each country's time-invariant traits and each year's EU-wide shocks.
:::

::: {.fs-80}
**In the IDE workspace:** the estimand statement in the callout "Task 2, continued" of `index.qmd`, with its gaps in brackets.
:::

::: notes
You wrote the estimand once already, on the slide with the template of Lundberg and colleagues, and here it is written out in full. The unit-specific quantity is the change in cosmopolitan framing within a country from one year to the next that goes with a one-point change in its unemployment rate, and the target population is the member states over the decade. In the aggregation, fixed effects make a choice for you, because the country-years whose unemployment departs most from their country and year means count most. In your report the statement has gaps in brackets, which you fill for this claim in your own words.
:::

## Hands-on 2 – The causal graph {#hands-on-2-the-causal-graph .smaller .output-8}

::: {.fs-80}
The committed arrows are live and the arguable ones commented out: take the `#` off any that you believe, run the graph, then its adjustment set.\
**In the IDE workspace:** `R/dag_starter.R`, then the chunks `dag` and `adjustment-set` of `index.qmd`.
:::

::: {.fs-70}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| max-lines: 8
my_dag <- dagify(
  # The path of interest, and the two common causes (country and year)
  # that two-way fixed effects absorb.
  framing      ~ unemployment,
  framing      ~ country,
  unemployment ~ country,
  framing      ~ year,
  unemployment ~ year,

  # GROWTH as a time-varying confounder: a slump raises unemployment and may
  # sour EU sentiment in the same year.
  # framing      ~ growth,
  # unemployment ~ growth,

  # BAILOUT as a mediator: unemployment triggers a financial-assistance
  # programme, which then shapes framing.
  # bailout ~ unemployment,
  # framing ~ bailout,

  # POLITICISATION of the EU by parties and elites as another cause of
  # framing. The robustness study instructed analysts to disregard it.
  # framing ~ politicisation,

  exposure = "unemployment",
  outcome  = "framing",
  # Coordinates of all seven nodes; those of a node that no arrow names are
  # ignored.
  coords = list(
    x = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 3, country = 1, year = 2,
          growth = 0.9, bailout = 1.5, politicisation = 3),
    y = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 0, country = 1.4, year = 1.4,
          growth = -1.0, bailout = -1.2, politicisation = -0.95)))
```
:::

::: {.fs-90}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
adjustmentSets(my_dag)
```
:::

::: notes
The graph is the one in the DAG starter script of your IDE workspace, written as one R formula per arrow, with the effect on the left of the tilde and the cause on the right, so that `framing ~ unemployment` is the arrow from unemployment to framing. The five committed arrows are live, and the arguable ones are commented out, one claim per line. [run both] With the committed arrows the adjustment set is country and year, which a two-way fixed-effects model absorbs. [uncomment the growth pair; run both] With growth as a confounder the set becomes country, growth and year, because a slump varies within a country over time and fixed effects cannot reach it, which is a finding about the design and not a bug in your code. The bailout pair makes a mediator, and the set does not grow.
:::
